title: Resilience Isn't About Toughing It Out
excerpt: Reframing resilience as flexibility and recovery, not just endurance.

value.text: Resilience has become one of those words that can quietly work against us. Somewhere along the way it came to mean toughness — the ability to grit your teeth, absorb whatever comes, and keep going no matter the cost. Under that definition, being resilient looks a lot like never stopping, never complaining, and never letting the strain show. Which is, if you think about it, a fairly reliable recipe for burning out.

Real resilience is something gentler and far more useful. It is not about how much you can endure without breaking. It is about how well you can bend, adapt, and recover — how flexibly you meet what life brings, and how reliably you find your way back to steadiness afterwards.
Endurance is not the same as resilience

Endurance is about persistence through strain: keeping going regardless. It has its place — sometimes you genuinely do need to get through a hard stretch. But endurance used as a permanent setting is exhausting, because it asks you to override your own signals indefinitely. Sooner or later the body sends the bill.

Resilience, by contrast, includes the capacity to stop. To notice you are stretched and adjust. To rest before you are forced to. Paradoxically, the people who bounce back most reliably are often the ones most willing to pause — because they are not spending all their energy holding a brittle position.

Think of a tree in a storm. The rigid trunk that refuses to move is the one that snaps; the one that bends with the wind survives. Flexibility is not weakness — it is what allows something to withstand force without breaking. Emotional flexibility works the same way.

items: Adjusting your expectations when circumstances change, rather than forcing the old plan through.
Allowing difficult feelings to move through you instead of bracing against them.
Asking for help as a strategy, not a last resort.
Letting how you respond be shaped by what the moment actually needs.

value.text: This kind of flexibility is a skill, not a personality trait. It can be practised, and it grows with attention — often most of all during the very periods of change that feel hardest.

The part of resilience most often left out is recovery. We celebrate the pushing through and quietly skip the coming back. But a nervous system that never gets to settle does not become stronger — it becomes chronically activated. Recovery is not what you earn after resilience; it is a core part of what resilience is.

This is why rest, regulation, and genuinely switching off are not indulgences but requirements. If the idea of resilience-as-toughness has ever left you feeling that stopping is somehow a failure, you may find it freeing to read why [resilience is not the same as toughing it out at work](/blog/switching-off-always-on-job), and how the early signs of running low ask to be heard rather than overridden — something explored in more depth in [these early signs of burnout](/blog/running-on-empty-early-signs-of-burnout).

Reframed this way, resilience stops being a demand to be superhuman and becomes something far more sustainable: the ability to move with change rather than brace against it, to recover well, and to stay in contact with yourself through the wobble. It is not about needing less support. It is about knowing when to reach for it.
The most resilient people are not the ones who never bend. They are the ones who bend, recover, and find their footing again.

If a season of change has you feeling stretched thin, that is not a lack of resilience — it may be resilience asking to be resourced. A [conversation about working together](/work-with-me) can be one steady place to start building the flexible, recoverable kind of strength that actually lasts.
